The Red filament threadfin bream (Nemipterus marginatus) attains a maximum standard length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters], though this value is notably larger than the 15 centimeter maximum reported in some field-based ichthyological surveys, a discrepancy that may reflect local environmental influences on growth. Reproductive maturity in this lutjaniform species is reached at a standard length of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters], marking the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the transition from the immature sub-adult phase to a reproductively viable state. Field records indicate that newly hatched larvae emerge from pelagic eggs that each carry a yolk reserve of approximately 0.5 millimeters in diameter; following complete yolk-sac resorption, the wet weight of the neonate at the point of first exogenous feeding is about 0.000066 grams [Wwb = about 0.000066 grams], a minute initial mass characteristic of small-bodied reef-associated teleosts. This modest birth mass imposes a narrow window for successful first prey capture before the point of no nutritional return is reached.

Adults of Nemipterus marginatus that have completed their somatic growth achieve an ultimate wet weight of approximately 119 grams [Wwi = approximately 119 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship typical of the species. This asymptotic mass is attained gradually, as individuals channel resources toward both structural growth and the accumulation of lipid stores essential for gametogenesis. At the onset of puberty, identified by the appearance of the first vitellogenic oocytes in females and active spermatogenesis in males, individuals weigh roughly 13 grams [Wwp = roughly 13 grams], indicating that a significant proportion of lifetime mass gain occurs after the initiation of reproductive capability. Under the stable thermal conditions of their tropical reef habitat, consistently measured at 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C], the maximum lifespan of Nemipterus marginatus is estimated at approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], a longevity that aligns with values observed in other iteroparous nemipterids of comparable body size.

At the same stable environmental temperature of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C], the reproductive output of Nemipterus marginatus has been characterized through studies on a congeneric species providing an indirect estimate for the red filament threadfin bream. Specifically, a female with a fork length of 23.75 centimeters near the upper end of the adult size range releases approximately 17,000 pelagic eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 17,000 pelagic eggs per spawning event] with spawning events recurring about every 50 days [F_R_i = events recurring about every 50 days] under these thermal conditions. This pattern reflects the high fecundity observed in other tropical demersal spawners that release multiple batches of pelagic eggs throughout an extended breeding season. The energetic investment implied by such sustained output is considerable necessitating efficient foraging on benthic invertebrates to meet the metabolic costs of gamete production.

The larval development of Nemipterus marginatus proceeds through the typical teleostean sequence following eclosion. After the yolk-sac larva completes the absorption of its endogenous reserves the exotrophic transition begins as the mouth opens and retinal differentiation enables first prey capture. The pelagic larval phase is protracted with preflexion and flexion-stage individuals drifting in the plankton where they feed on copepod nauplii and small zooplankton. Larval metamorphosis involving the allometric shift in body proportions and the onset of fin ray ossification culminates in the recruitment of post-metamorphic juveniles to demersal habitats. During this pelagic-benthic transition young individuals seek structured reef environments where they encounter both abundant prey and the cover necessary to evade predation. Mortality during the larval stage is exceptionally high a demographic reality that balances the elevated fecundity documented in the spawning adult population.

The interplay between the small birth mass of approximately 0.000066 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000066 grams] and the high fecundity of spawning adults has important demographic consequences for Nemipterus marginatus. The minute larval size necessitates abundant planktonic prey and brief critical periods for exogenous feeding to avoid starvation. However, the capacity for sustained high fecundity throughout a lifespan of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] at 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C] provides demographic resilience allowing the population to compensate for heavy early mortality. The asymptotic body mass of 119 grams [Wwi = 119 grams] and length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters] define a relatively small-bodied fish whose life history appears finely tuned to the productive warm waters of its tropical reef ecosystem. The 13 gram [Wwp = 13 gram] mass at the onset of gonadal activity compared to the ultimate adult mass suggests that reproductive capability emerges well before full somatic size is reached an adaptation that may buffer population-level reproductive output against interannual variability in resource availability.
